title: Europe puts a 9.5% anti-dumping duty on cold-rolled steel from India
subtitle: The European Union says this steel reached Europe too cheap, so it added an extra border tax. Here is what that means for Indian steel makers.
content_html:
Picture a giant roll of thin, shiny steel sheet, as heavy as a small truck, waiting at a port in Europe. If that roll came from India, its buyer now pays an extra 9.5% tax at the border. On Monday, 16 November 2026, the European Commission set a final anti-dumping duty of 9.5% on certain cold-rolled flat steel from India.

India is not alone. The same rule hits Japan (27.9%), Taiwan (20.7% to 27%), Türkiye (3% to 7.8%) and Vietnam (16%). The Commission also said this was the first case in which it found a "Particular Market Situation", and India is one of the two countries where it found one.

First, what is cold-rolled steel?

Steel first leaves a plant as thick, hot sheets. When those sheets are rolled again at room temperature, they turn thinner, smoother and neater. That is cold-rolled steel. Think of it as the tidy steel sheet that factories bend and press into the things people use every day. The Commission says this steel is used in most areas of manufacturing.

This steel matters a lot to Europe. The EU market for these products is worth about 23.2 billion euros. Europe's own makers run plants in 12 EU countries and employ over 8,600 people, the Commission says.

So what is dumping?

Imagine a samosa seller from another town who sells samosas in your colony for Rs 8 each, while he charges Rs 12 back home. The local samosa stall cannot match that price and starts losing customers. Selling abroad for less than at home is called dumping.

An anti-dumping duty is an extra tax at the border that lifts the low price back up, so local makers get a fair match. Say a coil of Indian steel costs a European buyer 100 euros at the border. With the new duty, that same coil now costs 109.50 euros.

How did Europe decide the steel was too cheap?

The probe began on 18 September 2025, after a complaint by Eurofer, the group of Europe's steel makers. It studied sales from July 2024 to June 2025, SteelOrbis reported.

In its findings shared in August 2026, the Commission said imports of this steel from the five countries grew 28% compared with 2022, to about 1.69 million tonnes. Their average price fell 34% to 695 euros a tonne. Indian steel sold for about 11% less than steel made by European companies. Over the same time, European makers' share of their own market slipped from 70% to 66%.

In cricket terms, it is like a visiting team scoring easy runs on a pitch the home side cannot play on. The home side complained, and the umpire agreed.

What is a "Particular Market Situation"?

Normally, to check for dumping, the Commission compares the price of steel inside the home country with the price charged in Europe. But if prices at home are bent out of shape, that test does not work. The Commission calls this a Particular Market Situation. When it finds one, it can build a fair home price of its own instead of using the real one.

For India, the Commission said government measures had affected the price of iron ore at home. Iron ore is a key raw material for this steel. For Taiwan, it pointed to cheap Chinese steel coming in and pulling down local prices.

The Commission called the case important for its trade defence work well beyond steel. In simple words, Europe now has one more tool it can use in future cases.

Which countries sell this steel to Europe?

The Commission's numbers show how big each country's sales are. Taiwan sent 345 million euros of this steel, India 282 million euros, Türkiye 240 million euros, Japan 180 million euros and Vietnam 125 million euros. Add them up and you get 1,172 million euros. India's part is about a quarter of that, the second biggest after Taiwan.

Steel from India now faces a lower duty than steel from Japan, Taiwan or Vietnam, but a higher one than any rate on Türkiye. Japan's rate of 27.9% is almost three times India's.

Why Europe matters so much to Indian steel

In 2025-26, India sent 6.6 million tonnes of finished steel abroad, 36% more than the year before, according to steel ministry data reported by Argus. Italy was the biggest single buyer, at 1.07 million tonnes. Italy, Belgium and Spain together took 34% of all the finished steel India sent abroad.

A 9.5% duty means a European buyer pays more for each Indian coil, unless the Indian seller lowers the price.

There is one small piece of good news for sellers. Europe did not set a short-term duty during the probe, so the final duty cannot be charged on steel that landed earlier, the Commission found in August.

One more cost on top of the carbon tax

Indian steel bound for Europe already deals with Europe's carbon border tax, called CBAM, and with yearly import limits called quotas. Argus reported that these rules had made European buyers more careful about Indian steel. The new duty adds one more cost on top.

What to watch next

The duty is now final. For Indian mills, two questions matter most. Will European buyers keep ordering at the higher price? And will mills send more of this steel to other countries instead? The answers will show up in the trade numbers over the coming months.
